newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - Commodities see more buoyant 1997.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Commodities see more buoyant 1997.

text.p: Expected lower interest rates and higher growth in most of the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) member countries should make 1997 a buoyant year for commodity markets, according to economists and market analysts.
However resultant higher demand will not mean higher prices across the commodity spectrum.
"Stock levels at the end of 1996 will mean some markets will respond more than others by higher offtake," one economist said.

Economists are looking for a growth rate averaging between 3.8 percent and four percent for the OECD in 1997 and that, coupled with real short term interest rates averaging around 4.5 percent in the OECD versus seven percent 18 months ago, also augurs well for accelerated economic activity.

"Translating that into orders is more debatable but I think it will happen. The whole cycle is moving. Now it is bonds and equities. Commodities will come back into fashion," said metals markets analyst Nick Moore at Fleming Global Mining group.
BASE METALS TO BENEFIT
Among the likely beneficiaries of the notch up in industrial activity will be the base metals aluminium, nickel and zinc.
"The metals that will do best are keyed into overall demand growth, principally aluminium and nickel. Clearly they do not have so onerous a supply burden," said Moore.

Zinc, too, could see demand growth pushing prices up next year. "It's not very glamorous but it is worth watching. At the end of the cycle people suddenly notice it and say "where did that come from?'", one analyst said.
But copper prices would be restrained by over-hanging stocks in the wake of Japanese conglomerate Sumitomo Corporation losing $2.6 billion in copper trading.
Rising output towards year end could also hamper nickel prices rises, analysts said.
Gold was likely to be burdened by the threat of central bank sales, producers selling forward to protect their prices and option trading hemming prices into a narrow band.
"If gold can break out of its options stranglehold, 1997 could be an extremely volatile year," said Ted Arnold, a vice president at Merrill Lynch in London.
He saw the bullion prices falling as far as $330 per ounce before price-sensitive Asia gold buyers were attracted.

Of the other precious metals, only palladium looked to have the industrial demand base to escape from gold's shadow. "Silver and platinum don't look fundamentally strong enough to pull out from gold," said metals markets analyst Tony Warwick-Ching at researchers CRU International.
"But palladium is seeing some substitution for platinum (in industrial uses) and there is scope for a more industrially-based recovery next year," he said.
COCOA, COFFEE OUTLOOK UNCERTAIN
The outlook for cocoa and coffee was uncertain and hung on upcoming crop outurns, according to brokers GNI commodity market analyst Lawrence Eagles.
"Theoretically cocoa could be heading for a dull year. But that depends on whether or not last year's huge West African crop was a freak of the weather," he said.

If the West African harvest returned to more normal levels, a deficit of 300,000 tonnes, representing about one-third of current world stocks, could be expected. "That will not be clear until mid-January," he said.
For coffee, the size of the Brazilian crop currently estimated at between 24 and 27 million 60-kg bags was the key.
"The market is tight already and so export limitations could continue and the price should rise next year," he said.
Sugar prices were likely to fall as high stocks in several producing countries were exported, he added.
GRAINS FACE MIXED YEAR
There is a mixed outlook too for grains in 1997, said economist Bill Demaria of the World Grain Council (WGC).
He was looking for a "modest increase" in offtake next year for wheat demand but coarse grains could be more dramatic.
Wheat demand would be well met during the first few months of 1997 by the continuing sale of Argentina's record crop.
"About half the Argentine crop is sold and until that is complete, there will be no firm change in the price," he said.
Stocks were likely to increase next year with wheat stores rising to 102 million tonnes from 95 million in 1995/96 and coarse grains rising to 114 million tonnes from 87 million tonnes last year.
A preliminary WGC forecast predicted a small increase in wheat production at 580 million to against 575 million tonnes in 1995/96, assuming normal weather, a WGC spokesman said.
